text: Colin Stephenson Pittendrigh (October 13, 1918 – March 19, 1996) was a British-born biologist who spent most of his adult life in the United States and is recognized as the "father of the biological clock," co-founding the modern field of chronobiology with Jürgen Aschoff and Erwin Bünning. Born in Whitley Bay, Northumberland (now Tyne and Wear), he earned his first degree in botany in 1940 from the University of Durham, now the University of Newcastle upon Tyne. During World War II, as a conscientious objector, he worked in Trinidad to improve fruit production for the UK and to control malaria by studying mosquito breeding in epiphytic bromeliad water tanks, where he observed daily rhythms in mosquito activity and noted that peak times varied by species and canopy level. This work sparked his interest in biological rhythms, leading to later studies on eclosion in Drosophila. He married Margaret "Mikey" Dorothy Eitelbach during the war and moved to Trinidad, where they lived in the rainforest and worked on malaria control; he returned to the U.S. in 1945. They had two children, Robin Rourk (now in Louisville, Colorado) and Colin Jr. (now in Bozeman), and Pittendrigh had a grandson and granddaughter. He was an avid fly fisherman and outdoorsman and retired to Bozeman, Montana, where he continued studying biological clocks and lectured at Montana State University – Bozeman. After the war, he earned his Ph.D. in biology from Columbia University under Theodosius Dobzhansky in 1947 and joined the Princeton faculty as an assistant professor, where he began his circadian rhythm research. He gained U.S. citizenship in 1950 and served as dean of graduate studies from 1965 to 1969, and was active on national scientific boards, including NASA’s Science Advisory Committee. In 1969, he moved to Stanford, where he helped establish the Human Biology program and served as director of the Hopkins Marine Station from 1976 to 1984, rebuilding the marine biology lab with modern molecular biology, ecology, and biomechanics. He retired from Stanford in 1984 and remained in Bozeman. In 1958, he met Aschoff, with whom he developed opposing models of entrainment: Aschoff proposed a parametric model where light alters the endogenous period (τ) and oscillation baseline, while Pittendrigh supported a nonparametric model where entrainment is sudden and daily, with a phase shift (Δφ) calculated by Δφ(φ) = τ – T. Despite their differences, they remained close friends and exchanged ideas throughout their lives. Pittendrigh established key criteria for a biological clock, demonstrating in Drosophila pseudoobscura that eclosion rhythms persist in constant conditions, are temperature-compensated, and can be entrained by light cycles near the natural period (τ). Beginning in 1958, he developed the phase response curve (PRC), which predicts how light changes affect biological rhythms; PRCs detected simultaneously in his and Woody Hastings' labs formed the basis for the nonparametric entrainment model. While the PRC accurately describes Drosophila rhythms, it fails to predict mammalian entrainment responses, especially when subjective day/night intervals are compressed, due to malleability of τ and the PRC during entrainment. Aschoff’s parametric model, though largely abandoned, helped explain limitations in Pittendrigh’s model. From 1964 to 1965, Pittendrigh co-chaired a National Academy committee on Mars exploration with Joshua Lederberg, investigating the possibility of life on Mars at Stanford and the Rockefeller Institute, and received a NASA exobiology grant to study circadian rhythms on biosatellites and Earth, though no later publications on this study were found. He also participated in the anti-contamination panel of the Committee on Space Research (COSPAR) to prevent Earth life from contaminating Mars. In 1966, he co-authored *Biology and the Exploration of Mars: Report of a Study*, summarizing the exobiology findings. With Serge Daan, he published five papers on nocturnal rodents' circadian pacemakers, including findings that a 15-minute light pulse during subjective night causes phase shifts, supporting nonparametric entrainment; that rodents with longer periods have larger advance zones in their PRCs, while those with shorter periods have larger delay zones, implying diurnal organisms like humans have larger advance zones; and that a two-pulse system (one flash at dawn, one at dusk) mimics changing photoperiods, causing a phase jump when daylength exceeds 12 hours, supporting Aschoff’s parametric model; and that under constant high light, hamster locomotor activity splits into two components, leading to the E & M (Evening and Morning) dual oscillator model, where oscillators uncouple and free-run with different periods, with interactions depending on peak proximity, and which aligns with Aschoff’s Rules and aftereffects. Molecular evidence supports this model, such as in Drosophila, where PDF-producing cells drive morning activity without affecting evening peaks, and in mammals, where split hamsters show anti-phase SCN activity. Later, he studied temperature dependence of photoperiodic responses in Drosophila, developing the Photo-Periodic Response Curve (PPRC), and proposed a dual oscillator model where one oscillator is light-sensitive and the other is temperature-sensitive, explaining entrainment responses to light and dampened responses to temperature changes. He also collaborated with Knopka on drosophila per mutants, which have impaired temperature dependence, indicating reduced activity in the temperature oscillator, further supporting the temperature-light dual model system.
